questions.q: Why does this lesson say running a program once with a single input doesn't actually count as testing it?
options: Because Apex requires every program to be run exactly five times
Because it only tells you the code works for that one input, and a method that handles a normal case fine might still fail silently on zero, a negative number, or an unusually large input
Because a single run always takes too long to complete
Because System.debug cannot be used more than once per program
questions.explain: The lesson's opening point is that one successful run only tells you about that specific input -- genuine testing requires deliberately checking multiple scenarios most likely to reveal a bug.

questions.q: What is the difference between a boundary case and an edge case, per this lesson?
options: A boundary case is a value right at the edge of what's valid (like testing orderTotal at exactly 100); an edge case is an unusual but legitimate input like zero, a negative number, or null
There is no difference -- they are the same thing
A boundary case only applies to Strings, and an edge case only applies to Integers
An edge case is always an invalid input that should crash the program
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes boundary cases (values at the edge of a valid range, like testing exactly 100, 99, and 101 against a >= 100 threshold) from edge cases (unusual but legitimate inputs like zero, negative numbers, or null).

questions.q: What does the `@IsTest` annotation do in Apex, per this lesson?
options: It deletes the class it's attached to after one use
It converts a class into a Salesforce object
It automatically fixes any bugs found during testing
It marks a class and its methods as test-only code, not part of the application's real logic
questions.explain: The lesson states @IsTest marks a class and its methods as test-only code, distinct from the application's actual logic, previewed here ahead of the later Apex-focused course that covers testing in depth.

questions.q: What test-coverage rule does Salesforce enforce for deploying Apex code to a production org, per this lesson?
options: 100% test coverage with no exceptions
At least 50% test coverage
At least 75% test coverage
Salesforce has no test coverage requirement at all
questions.explain: The lesson states Apex code generally must have at least 75% test coverage to be deployed to a production org, a concrete platform rule beyond just being good general practice.

questions.q: Why does this lesson warn against treating the 75% coverage number itself as the goal?
options: Because code can hit 75% coverage with shallow tests that never check a boundary or edge case, giving a false sense of safety -- genuine coverage should come from testing the scenarios most likely to break
Because the number is not actually enforced by Salesforce
Because 75% coverage is impossible to achieve in practice
Because coverage percentage is unrelated to System.assertEquals
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly warns that chasing the percentage with shallow tests creates a false sense of safety -- the right goal is genuinely testing likely-to-break scenarios, with the percentage following as a side effect.
